name: Ice, Air and Evidence: How We Learned the Climate Changes
description: Ice ages, a cold summer, a Swedish calculation and a curve from a Hawaiian mountain: the clues scientists pieced together before the world agreed to act.

checkpoints.name: Ice and cold years
checkpoints.note: Earth has swung between ice ages and warm spells. The Last Glacial Maximum, the Younger Dryas and the Little Ice Age left traces, and the cold year of 1816 after a volcanic eruption showed how fragile harvests were.

checkpoints.name: Heat-trapping gases
checkpoints.note: Agassiz argued for vanished ice sheets and Hutton's deep time was widely accepted. Factories and steam engines burned coal, oil drilling began, and Arrhenius calculated that more carbon dioxide would warm the planet.

checkpoints.name: Smoke and dust
checkpoints.note: The Dust Bowl, the Great Smog of London and the spread of pesticides such as DDT made the cost of human activity visible, and scientists began to ask what humanity was doing to the air.

checkpoints.name: Counting the carbon
checkpoints.note: Keeling's Mauna Loa measurements showed carbon dioxide rising year by year. Rachel Carson's Silent Spring and the rise of Greenpeace made environmental worry political, and the Montreal Protocol healed the ozone layer.

checkpoints.name: Agreeing to act
checkpoints.note: The IPCC gathered the evidence. Kyoto and the Paris Agreement set targets, as the Pinatubo eruption tested climate models, wind and solar power grew, and the Anthropocene gained wide use as a name.
